about.title: Mesopotamia III: Trade, Everyday Life and Empires
about.length_note: About 40 minutes. The class has five topics, each taught in short steps with a check question. It can be split into two sittings, with a natural break after the trade section (before 'Empires'). Learners who pause to think over the questions will take a little longer.

say.text: Welcome to class three. So far we have met the first cities, writing and law. Today: how people lived, what they traded, and how cities grew into empires.

show.text: Mesopotamia III: Trade, Everyday Life and Empires

say.text: We will go one step at a time: daily life, trade, empires, then numbers and the calendar, and last, what was happening elsewhere. You can pause any time.

show.text:
1. A day in the life
2. Trade
3. From city-states to empires
4. Numbers, calendar, technology
5. The wider world at the same time

say.text: First idea: the ration. A ration is a fixed share of food or drink given as pay. In cities, many people stopped growing their own food and lived on wages or rations.

show.text: Ration = a fixed share of food or drink given as pay

say.text: Here is an example. Temples gave their workers a daily ration of barley beer, the staple drink of Mesopotamia.

show.text: Illustration: a temple worker holds out a bowl while an official pours barley beer from a large clay jar.

ask.q: What is a ration?
ask.right: A fixed share of food or drink given as pay
wrong: A tax paid to the king
ask.why: Workers were paid in wages or rations, such as a daily share of barley beer from the temple.

say.text: Farming did not disappear when cities grew. Farmers grew wheat, barley, lentils, onions, dates and grapes. They kept cattle, sheep, goats and pigs.

show.text:
Crops: wheat, barley, lentils, onions, dates, grapes
Animals: cattle, sheep, goats, pigs

say.text: Most people ate two meals a day, one before work in the morning and one after work in the evening. Bread, beer and onions were the staples.

ask.q: How many meals a day did most people eat?
ask.right: Two
ask.why: Most people ate one meal in the morning before work and one in the evening after work.

say.text: The evening meal might be vegetable stew or fish soup, with roast mutton or lamb on special days. Beer was the favourite drink, even for rich people who could afford wine.

show.text: Illustration: a family around a bowl of vegetable stew, with flat bread, onions and a jar of beer.

say.text: Next, houses. Most were built of sun-dried mud brick, with rooms around an open courtyard. Walls were plastered and whitewashed inside and out. Roofs were flat, and families slept up there when it was hot. The white walls helped reflect the heat of the sun.

show.text: Illustration: a mud-brick house with a central courtyard, whitewashed walls and a flat roof with a bed on it.

ask.q: Why were the walls whitewashed?
ask.right: To help reflect the heat
wrong: To show which gods the family followed
To stop the river flooding the house
ask.why: The whitewash helped reflect heat, which mattered in a hot climate.

say.text: Homes showed wealth. Rich families had large, multi-storey mud-brick houses with separate rooms. Ordinary families had smaller one-storey homes with simple furnishings.

show.text: Wealthy: large, several storeys, open courtyard, separate rooms || Ordinary: smaller, one storey, simple furniture

say.text: Now family. Marriages were often arranged, and the household was usually patriarchal. That means the father held the authority.

show.text: Patriarchal = the father holds the authority in the family

say.text: What did women do? Most worked at home, caring for the family. Some worked as weavers, potters, tavern-keepers or bakers. Women and children also worked in the textile industry.

show.text: At home: caring for the family, cooking, grinding grain || For work: weaving, pottery, tavern-keeping, baking, textiles

say.text: Women also had some rights. In some periods, for example in Sumer, women could own property and take part in business.

show.text: Some Sumerian women: property and business rights

ask.q: Which statement fits the sources we have just heard?
ask.right: In some periods, women in Sumer could own property and take part in business
wrong: Women were never allowed to work for pay
Only men could ever bake bread
ask.why: Sources describe a father-led household, but also women who owned property and did business in some periods.

say.text: Now put it together as a day. First, a farm family. Most commoners were farmers living outside the city walls. Women were up by sunrise to make breakfast.

show.text:
Sunrise: breakfast of porridge, bread and beer
Morning: work outside
Midday: bread and beer carried as a snack
Evening: main meal
After dinner: singing and storytelling

say.text: A city worker's day was different. City people could earn their living in industry, trade or administration, paid by wages or rations. A mother might grind grain while a child played with a clay toy pig with beads inside.

show.text: Illustration: a woman grinding grain at a stone, a child beside her shaking a hollow clay pig.

ask.q: What mainly marked a city worker's day, compared with a farmer's?
ask.right: They earned wages or rations instead of growing most of their own food
wrong: They lived only on the roof
They were forbidden to work with their hands
ask.why: City life brought many kinds of work, and urban people were paid in wages or rations.

say.text: In rich homes, the first people up were slaves or servants, who got the meal ready. Slaves were one of the groups that lived in the cities.

show.text: Illustration: a servant stoking a cooking fire early in a large house while the family sleeps.

ask.q: In a wealthy home, who was usually up first to prepare breakfast?
ask.right: Slaves or servants
ask.why: In wealthy homes, slaves or servants prepared the meal. In ordinary homes, the women did.

say.text: Evenings could be lively. Clay plaques show people with drums and rattles, and families sang and told stories after dinner.

show.text: Illustration: a plaque-style scene of two musicians, one with a drum and one with a rattle.

say.text: Now trade. The river valley gave good farmland. But metals and fine stones came from far away, even from lands thousands of kilometres off.

show.text: Trade: getting what you do not have

say.text: Take lapis lazuli, a deep blue stone prized for beads and seals. As far as anyone can tell, it all came from mines in Badakhshan, in modern Afghanistan. That is about 2,400 kilometres, or 1,500 miles, east.

show.text: 2,400 km from the lapis mines to Mesopotamia

ask.q: Where did Mesopotamia's lapis lazuli come from?
ask.right: Mines in what is now Afghanistan
ask.why: Lapis lazuli found in the ancient Near East appears to come from mines in Badakhshan, in modern Afghanistan.

say.text: Sumerian texts name three lands they traded with: Magan, Dilmun and Meluhha. Dilmun lay in the Persian Gulf, Magan is usually placed in Oman, and Meluhha is probably the Indus Valley.

show.text: Map: Mesopotamia at the top of the Persian Gulf. Dilmun in the Gulf, Magan to the south-east in Oman, Meluhha far to the east (probably the Indus Valley), and the Badakhshan mountains to the north-east.

say.text: Dilmun was an entrepôt, a meeting point where goods change hands. It did not make most of the goods. Mesopotamian goods were swapped there for goods from Magan and Meluhha.

show.text: Entrepôt = a meeting point where goods change hands

ask.q: What is an entrepôt?
ask.right: A meeting point where goods change hands
wrong: A royal storehouse for tax grain
ask.why: Dilmun was an entrepôt: goods from Mesopotamia were traded there for goods from Magan and Meluhha.

say.text: Magan was called the land of copper, and was probably the main copper source for the Sumerians. Before about 1000 BCE, copper was the cheapest and most widely used metal in Mesopotamia.

show.text: Magan = land of copper

say.text: Meluhha sent timber, ivory, lapis lazuli, gold and carnelian. In return, Mesopotamia sent things like silver, tin and woollen textiles. Scholars are less sure of the full list.

show.text: Came to Mesopotamia: timber, ivory, lapis lazuli, gold, carnelian, pearls || Went out: silver, tin, woollen textiles, perhaps oil and grain

ask.q: Which of these did Mesopotamia send out in trade?
ask.right: Woollen textiles
ask.why: Ivory, carnelian and lapis lazuli came in. Woollen textiles, silver and tin went out.

say.text: How do we know the sea trade was real? Round stamped seals in a Persian Gulf style turned up in Mesopotamia, at Lothal in India, and on Failaka island. That is good evidence of long sea routes.

show.text: Photo-style image: a small round stamp seal with animal designs, shown beside a clay impression.

say.text: A different route went north by land. Merchants from the city of Ashur led donkey caravans to Anatolia, in modern Turkey. They sold tin and textiles, and took back silver, gold and copper.

show.text: Illustration: a line of laden donkeys led along a mountain track by two merchants.

ask.q: What did the Old Assyrian merchants mainly sell in Anatolia?
ask.right: Tin and textiles
ask.why: They exported tin and textiles and received silver, gold and copper.

say.text: Their main trading town was Kanesh, today called Kültepe. The Assyrian trading quarter was called a karum, a word that first meant a quay. Over 23,000 clay tablets have been dug up there, mostly from about 1950 to 1840 BCE.

show.text: Photo-style image: clay tablets in envelopes of clay, from the archive at Kanesh (Kültepe).

say.text: Trade had rules. Merchants paid taxes on imports, exports and tolls along the road. The karum could fix prices and settle debts. Copper and silver acted as money.

show.text:
Taxes: import, export and road tolls
The karum: fixes prices, settles debts
Money: copper and silver

ask.q: What was a karum?
ask.right: A trading outpost where merchants lived and did business
ask.why: A karum was an Assyrian trade outpost, with Kanesh as the most important.

say.text: Now empires. At first, each city ran itself as a city-state. An empire puts many cities and peoples under one ruler. In the Mesopotamian story, Sargon was the first to do it.

show.text: City-state: one city runs itself || Empire: one ruler over many cities and peoples

say.text: Sargon of Akkad ruled from about 2334 to 2279 BCE. He took all southern Mesopotamia and parts of Syria, Anatolia and Elam, and made the city of Akkad his capital.

show.text: c. 2334 BCE: Sargon begins to rule || c. 2279 BCE: Sargon dies

say.text: How did he hold it together? He sent Akkadian governors to rule Sumerian cities and tore down their defensive walls. He left Sumerian religion alone but made Akkadian the official language.

show.text:
Akkadian governors in each city
City defensive walls torn down
Sumerian religion left in place
Akkadian as the official language

ask.q: How did Sargon keep control of the cities he took?
ask.right: He sent Akkadian governors to rule them
wrong: He let each city keep its own army and walls
He moved every citizen to Akkad
ask.why: Sargon replaced local rule with Akkadian governors and removed city defensive walls.

say.text: This helped trade too. Fewer walls and one language made trade easier. Sargon's own inscription mentions ships from Meluhha, Magan and Dilmun.

show.text: Ships from Meluhha, Magan and Dilmun (Sargon's inscription)

say.text: Now a site with a twist: the city of Akkad itself. Sargon either founded or restored it, around 2334 BCE. But archaeologists have never found it. It was probably on the Euphrates between Sippar and Kish.

show.text: Map-style image: the Euphrates with Kish and Sippar marked, and a question mark between them for Akkad.

ask.q: Has the city of Akkad been found?
ask.right: No, its location is still unknown
wrong: Yes, it was dug up in the 1800s
Yes, its ruins are fully mapped
Only its temple has been found
ask.why: Akkad, the capital of the first empire, has not yet been located.

say.text: The empire did not last. When Sargon died, there were revolts. In all, the Akkadian dynasty held on for about two hundred years. His grandson Naram-Sin was one of the later rulers.

show.text: Akkadian Empire: about 200 years

say.text: Babylon's turn came later. When Hammurabi became king in 1792 BCE, his kingdom was only four cities: Babylon, Kish, Sippar and Borsippa. By 1750 BCE he held the whole region.

ask.q: How many cities made up Hammurabi's kingdom when he began?
ask.right: Four
ask.why: Babylon, Kish, Sippar and Borsippa. Through campaigns and alliances he held the whole region by 1750 BCE.

say.text: After Hammurabi died, Babylonia declined. In 1595 BCE a Hittite king unseated its ruler, and the Kassites from the east took power for 400 years. His famous law code was in class two.

show.text: 1792–1750 BCE: Hammurabi || 1595 BCE: Hittite king ends the dynasty || then Kassite rule (400 years)

say.text: Assyria had two big chapters. The first was the merchants we met. The second was the Neo-Assyrian Empire, about 912 to 612 BCE. It took Babylonia in 729 BCE, and the Assyrian king became king of Babylon too.

show.text: c. 912 BCE: Neo-Assyrian Empire || 729 BCE: Assyria takes Babylonia || 612 BCE: Nineveh falls

say.text: Its last great king, Ashurbanipal, ruled from 668 to 627 BCE from the capital Nineveh. He built a library. It was made in the 600s BCE, and Nineveh was sacked in 612 BCE, when the library burned.

show.text: Illustration: shelves of clay tablets in a palace room in Nineveh, a scribe reading one.

say.text: Here is the twist. Clay tablets were usually not fired. But the fire that destroyed Nineveh baked many of them hard, so they survived. In the mid-1800s, Austen Henry Layard found them. Over 30,000 texts have been recovered.

show.text: Over 30,000 texts found in the 1800s

ask.q: When was Ashurbanipal's library found by archaeologists?
ask.right: In the mid-1800s, by Austen Henry Layard
wrong: In the 600s BCE, when it was built
ask.why: The library was built in the 600s BCE and burned in 612 BCE. It was found again in the mid-1800s.

say.text: Another Nineveh find: stone wall carvings showing the Assyrian siege of Lachish in 701 BCE. Layard found them in 1847.

show.text: Photo-style image: a stone relief of Assyrian soldiers attacking a walled hill town.

say.text: Then Babylon rose again. Nabopolassar began the Neo-Babylonian Empire in 626 BCE and led the conquest of Assyria. Nebuchadnezzar II ruled 605 to 562 BCE. He built the Ishtar Gate and great walls of Babylon around 575 BCE.

show.text: 626 BCE: Nabopolassar becomes king of Babylon || 605–562 BCE: Nebuchadnezzar II || c. 575 BCE: Ishtar Gate

say.text: The end came in 539 BCE. The Persian king Cyrus the Great took Babylon, and the older cuneiform record says his army entered without a battle.

show.text: 539 BCE: Cyrus of Persia takes Babylon

say.text: Here is how long three of these empires lasted, in rough years. The dates for the starts and ends come from the sources shown.

show.text: How long each empire lasted

ask.q: Which of these three empires lasted longest, going by the chart?
ask.right: The Neo-Assyrian Empire
wrong: They all lasted the same time
ask.why: Neo-Assyria is about 300 years, Akkad about 180, and Neo-Babylon about 87.

say.text: A pattern appears. The rulers conquered cities, sent governors, used one official language and encouraged trade. Then revolts or outside powers brought the empires down.

show.text:
Conquest
Governors from the centre
One official language
More trade
Then: revolt or outside conquest

say.text: Now numbers. Mesopotamian scribes counted in base 60, called sexagesimal. Each place in a number was worth 60 times the one before. We count in base 10.

show.text: Sexagesimal = base 60

say.text: Two signs wrote the numbers. An upright wedge meant 1, and a wedge head meant 10. Repeat them to reach 59. Ten plus one is 11. Sixty plus ten plus one reads as 71.

show.text:
Upright wedge = 1
Wedge head = 10
Repeat signs up to 59
60 + 10 + 1 = 71

ask.q: Two wedge heads and three upright wedges. What number is that?
ask.why: Two tens make 20, and three ones make 3, so 20 + 3 = 23.

say.text: We still use this. Base 60 shapes how we measure time and angles. That is why an hour has 60 minutes.

show.text: 60 minutes in an hour

say.text: A famous tablet is Plimpton 322. It was written around 1800 BCE, in the Old Babylonian period. One study dates it to 1822–1784 BCE. It holds a table of numbers in base 60.

show.text: Photo-style image: a broken clay tablet, about 13 by 9 centimetres, with columns of wedge-shaped numbers.

say.text: It was found in the early 1900s in what is now southern Iraq, by Edgar Banks. Today it is held at Columbia University. Experts still debate what it was for.

show.text: Made c. 1800 BCE. Found early 1900s.

ask.q: When was Plimpton 322 found?
ask.right: In the early 1900s
ask.why: It was written about 1800 BCE but found again in the early 1900s.

say.text: Now the calendar. It followed the Moon. A month began with the first sign of the new Moon and lasted 29 or 30 days. Twelve such months make 354 days.

show.text: Lunar month = 29 or 30 days

say.text: But a solar year is about 365 days. So twelve lunar months fall about eleven days short. Look at the gap.

show.text: Days in a year

say.text: The fix was to add a thirteenth month every few years, to keep in step with the seasons. This is called intercalation. Month names came from farm or religious tasks and differed by city. A regular 19-year pattern was found only around 400 BCE.

show.text: Intercalation = adding an extra month

ask.q: Why did Mesopotamians add an extra month every few years?
ask.right: To keep the calendar in step with the seasons
wrong: To make the months equal in length
ask.why: Twelve lunar months are about eleven days shorter than a solar year, so an extra month kept the seasons aligned.

say.text: A word on technology. The potter's wheel appeared in Mesopotamia in the 5th millennium BCE. The wheeled vehicle followed in the early 4th millennium BCE. Copper was the everyday metal.

show.text:
5th millennium BCE: potter's wheel
Early 4th millennium BCE: wheeled vehicle
Copper: everyday metal

say.text: Last, the wider world. Around 2600 BCE the Great Pyramid was built in Egypt. Harappa and Mohenjo-daro were flourishing in the Indus. Caral in Peru was being settled.

show.text: c. 2600 BCE: Great Pyramid built (Egypt) || 2600–1900 BCE: Indus civilization || c. 2600 BCE onward: Caral inhabited (Peru) || 2334–2279 BCE: Sargon || c. 1900–1500 BCE: Erlitou culture (China) || 1792–1750 BCE: Hammurabi || 605 BCE: Babylon defeats Egypt at Carchemish || 539 BCE: Cyrus takes Babylon

ask.q: Around 2600 BCE, what was being built in Egypt?
ask.right: The Great Pyramid of Giza
ask.why: The Great Pyramid dates to about 2600 BCE. The Ishtar Gate (about 575 BCE), the library (600s BCE) and the Lachish scene (701 BCE) are much later.

say.text: To finish: daily life was bread, beer and work. Trade reached Afghanistan and the Indus. Empires rose and fell. Let us check the order of four kings and rulers.

show.text:
Daily life: bread, beer, mud-brick houses, wages and rations
Trade: copper, lapis lazuli, tin, textiles, silver
Empires: Akkad, Babylon, Assyria, Neo-Babylon
Maths and calendar: base 60 and a Moon-led year

ask.q: Which order is right, earliest to latest?
ask.right: Sargon, Hammurabi, Ashurbanipal, Cyrus takes Babylon
wrong: Hammurabi, Sargon, Cyrus takes Babylon, Ashurbanipal
Ashurbanipal, Sargon, Hammurabi, Cyrus takes Babylon
Sargon, Ashurbanipal, Hammurabi, Cyrus takes Babylon
ask.why: Sargon began about 2334 BCE, Hammurabi in 1792 BCE, Ashurbanipal in 668 BCE, and Cyrus took Babylon in 539 BCE.

notes.topic: Gap to fill: the sources read for this class give no date for the first excavation of Kanesh (Kültepe) or for the rediscovery of the Ishtar Gate. Add both before publishing the 'built and found' pairs for those sites.

frame_of_reference.elsewhere: The Great Pyramid of Giza was built in Egypt. The Indus cities were flourishing, and Caral in Peru was being settled.
The Indus civilization was in its core period (about 2600–1900 BCE), and Caral was still inhabited.

frame_of_reference.when: c. 1950–1840 BCE (Assyrian trade at Kanesh) and 1792–1750 BCE (Hammurabi)
frame_of_reference.elsewhere: The Erlitou culture of ancient China is dated to roughly 1900–1500 BCE.
Nebuchadnezzar defeated an Egyptian army under Pharaoh Necho II at Carchemish.
The Persian king Cyrus the Great took Babylon, ending the Neo-Babylonian Empire.

other_side.claim: The Akkadian Empire was the first empire in the world.
other_side.other_view: The title is common, but the size and reach of the Akkadian Empire are disputed. Its capital Akkad has never been found, and a few early kings with Semitic names appear in older king lists.

other_side.claim: Women in Mesopotamia had a limited, home-based role.
other_side.other_view: Sources say the household was father-led and most women worked at home. They also say that in some periods, such as in Sumer, women owned property and did business.

other_side.claim: Houses were two or three storeys high.
other_side.other_view: One source says most city houses had two or three storeys. Another says commoners' houses were one or two. A third says ordinary people lived in single-storey homes and the rich in multi-storey ones. Height probably varied by wealth, place and period.

other_side.claim: Meluhha was the Indus Valley, and the goods traded are known.
other_side.other_view: Meluhha is only 'probably' the Indus Valley. One source says it was perhaps as far as the Indus. Another says the goods are less certain than the evidence for the sea route itself.

other_side.claim: Plimpton 322 is a Pythagorean-triples table, a trigonometry table, or something else.
other_side.other_view: Scholars have long disagreed about its purpose. Some see Pythagorean triples. Others reject a trigonometric reading. A 2017 UNSW team argues it is the world's oldest and most accurate trigonometric table, using ratios rather than angles. Dating also varies: one study gives 1822–1784 BCE, another about 1700 BCE.

One source gives 1849 for Layard's discovery, another gives 1850, and another says Layard and Rassam worked there between 1850 and 1853. Excavations continued for decades, so no single date is certain.
